content: Gatifloxacin, marketed as ZYMAXID®, is intended strictly for topical ophthalmic use and must not be introduced directly into the anterior chamber of the eye. Prolonged use of this medication, as with other anti-infective agents, may lead to the overgrowth of organisms that are not susceptible to the drug, including fungi. If a superinfection develops, the medication should be discontinued, and alternative therapy should be initiated. Clinical evaluation, including the use of magnification tools such as slit-lamp biomicroscopy and fluorescein staining, should be performed when deemed necessary by the clinician. Patients should be instructed to avoid wearing contact lenses if they exhibit signs or symptoms of bacterial conjunctivitis or while undergoing treatment with ZYMAXID®. Pregnancy ZYMAXID® is classified as Pregnancy Category C. Studies in rats and rabbits have not demonstrated teratogenic effects at oral doses up to 50 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 1000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. However, doses of 150 mg/kg/day or higher in rats (approximately 3000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose) have been associated with skeletal and craniofacial malformations, delayed ossification, atrial enlargement, and reduced fetal weight. In perinatal and postnatal studies, doses of 200 mg/kg/day (approximately 4000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose) resulted in increased late post-implantation loss and neonatal/perinatal mortality. Due to the lack of adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, ZYMAXID® should only be used during pregnancy if the potential benefits outweigh the potential risks to the fetus. Nursing Mothers Gatifloxacin has been shown to be excreted in the breast milk of rats. It is unknown whether the drug is excreted in human breast milk. Given that many drugs are excreted in human milk, caution is advised when administering ZYMAXID® to nursing mothers. Pediatric Use The safety and efficacy of ZYMAXID® in infants under one year of age have not been established. However, clinical trials have demonstrated that ZYMAXID® is safe and effective for treating bacterial conjunctivitis in pediatric patients aged one year and older. Geriatric Use No significant differences in safety or efficacy have been observed between elderly and younger patients treated with ZYMAXID®. Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, and Impairment of Fertility Long-term studies in B6C3F1 mice and Fischer 344 rats have shown no increase in neoplasms at dietary doses of gatifloxacin up to 1600to 2800-fold higher than the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. However, a statistically significant increase in large granular lymphocyte (LGL) leukemia was observed in male Fischer 344 rats at doses approximately 2000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose. This strain of rats has a high spontaneous background rate of LGL leukemia, and the observed incidence only slightly exceeded the historical control range for this strain. In genetic toxicity studies, gatifloxacin was positive in one of five bacterial reverse mutation assays (Salmonella strain TA102) and in in vitro mammalian cell mutation and chromosome aberration assays. It was also positive in in vitro unscheduled DNA synthesis assays in rat hepatocytes but not in human leukocytes. However, gatifloxacin was negative in in vivo micronucleus tests in mice, cytogenetics tests in rats, and DNA repair tests in rats. These findings may be attributed to the inhibitory effects of high concentrations of gatifloxacin on eukaryotic type II DNA topoisomerase. No adverse effects on fertility or reproduction were observed in rats given oral doses of gatifloxacin up to 200 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 4000 times the maximum recommended ophthalmic dose for ZYMAXID®.
